notes.h: Nodal regions and the idea of a node
notes.b: A nodal region is a city together with the surrounding area linked to it by flows of people, goods, services and information. Unlike the other regions in this chapter, it is defined by connections, not by uniform features.
points: A node is a central point where routes meet by road, rail, sea or air, usually a town or city. Think of it as the hub that the surrounding area is connected to.
A nodal region is also called a functional, city or urban region. It is functional because it is defined by what the links to the centre do, not by everything in it being the same.
A hinterland is the area around a town or city that it serves and depends on for jobs, shopping, services and markets. It is also called its sphere of influence or urban field.
The urban area is the continuously built-up part of the city, with houses and streets running on without a break. The hinterland extends far beyond it, into countryside and smaller towns.
The commuter belt is the part of the hinterland from which people travel daily to work in the city (commuting means making that regular journey).
notes.tip: A nodal region is a functional region, not a formal one, so never describe it as an area where everything is the same. True/false questions say the hinterland is the area around a town or city that it serves (true) and that a nodal region is characterised by poor transport (false, it has good transport).

notes.h: How a city and its hinterland interact
notes.b: A city and its hinterland depend on each other. Four kinds of flow tie them together: jobs, services, goods and information.
points: Jobs: commuters travel in from the hinterland every day, because the city has the workplaces and the hinterland has many of the workers.

Services: the city provides shops, hospitals, third-level colleges (universities and similar colleges), entertainment and offices that smaller places cannot support, and people from the hinterland travel in to use them.
Goods: the hinterland supplies food, water, raw materials and labour (workers); the city supplies manufactured goods and services in return.
A port's hinterland is the area whose trade passes through it, so goods from that area are exported, and goods for it imported, through that port.
Information: local newspapers, radio and TV stations based in the city serve the hinterland around it.
notes.tip: If asked to examine the relationship between a city and its hinterland, work through jobs, services, goods and information, giving what flows each way. This kind of 30-mark question is in syllabus scope.

notes.b: A hinterland has no marked border, so geographers work out where it ends by tracing where a city's services and links reach. Each method below gives a picture of the area.
points: Commuting data from the census (the official count of the population, which records where people travel to work) show how far workers come from.
The catchment area of a hospital, college or secondary school is the area from which it draws its patients or students.
The circulation area of a local newspaper (where it is sold) or the reach of a local radio station (where it can be heard) shows where the city's information flows.
Bus and rail routes and timetables show which places are linked to the city and how often.
The delivery areas of businesses, and the home addresses of shoppers or of members of a sports club, show who uses the city's shops and clubs and where they live.
The edge of a hinterland is not a sharp line: neighbouring hinterlands overlap, and different services give different boundaries, since a hospital and a newspaper do not reach the same distance.
Larger cities have larger hinterlands. A capital city's hinterland for some services is the whole country.
notes.tip: Remember that the edge of a hinterland is not a sharp line. Say that hinterlands overlap and that different services give different boundaries.

notes.b: Hinterlands are not fixed. Changes in transport, work and shopping can stretch them or squeeze them.
points: Motorways, car ownership, faster rail and remote working (working from home, so fewer daily trips) extend commuter belts outwards, because people can live further from the city and still reach it.
New shopping centres or services in smaller towns can shrink a city's hinterland, because people no longer need to travel to the city to use them.

notes.h: Dublin: a primate city and its hinterland
notes.b: A primate city is the largest city in a country, far larger than any other. Dublin is Ireland's primate city and capital: County Dublin has about 1.45 million people out of a State total of about 5.1 million (Census 2022).
points: It is the focus of the national motorway network: radial routes (roads spreading out from the centre like spokes) meet at the M50 ring road, which circles the city. The main rail lines also meet there.
Dublin Port and Dublin Airport, Ireland's busiest airport, make the city the main national gateway (entry and exit point) for trade and travel.

The commuter belt extends into Meath, Kildare, Wicklow and Louth, with fast-growing commuter towns (towns where many residents work in the city): Navan (Co. Meath), Naas and Newbridge (Co. Kildare), Bray (Co. Wicklow) and Drogheda (Co. Louth).
For government, national media, specialist hospitals and the main airport, Dublin's hinterland is the whole country, because these functions exist in Dublin and nowhere else on the same scale.
Problems of its urban region: urban sprawl (the built-up area spreading outwards into the countryside), long commutes and congestion, and high house prices.
There is more on the growth of city regions and Dublin's council structures in the European Regions chapter, and on land use and planning in the Urban Geography chapter.
notes.tip: In matching questions, a named city such as Dublin, Limerick, Milan or London is the urban region. Do not give population figures for Dublin city and suburbs.

notes.b: Outside Dublin, Ireland's other cities act as smaller nodes, each serving its own hinterland.
points: Cork: Ireland's second city, at the head of Cork Harbour on the River Lee.
Cork Harbour has a port and a pharmaceutical industry (making medicines), with plants at Ringaskiddy. Cork's hinterland covers much of Munster, with commuter towns Carrigaline, Midleton and Cobh.
Galway: the main city of the West, serving a large rural hinterland that includes Connemara.
Galway is a centre of the medical devices industry (making equipment used in healthcare) and of higher education (study after secondary school), home to the University of Galway.
Limerick and Waterford are regional cities serving the Mid-West and the South-East.
notes.tip: Do not give population figures for Cork, Limerick, Galway or Waterford.

notes.h: Planning to balance Irish city regions
notes.b: Dublin is so much larger than every other Irish city that national planning tries to even things out.
points: The National Planning Framework, part of Project Ireland 2040 and published in 2018, aims to direct more growth to Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford to counterbalance Dublin (to offset its dominance by building up the other cities).

notes.b: Cities across Europe are nodes with hinterlands of different sizes. Some reach across a whole country, and one crosses national borders.
points: Paris is the primate city of France, at the centre of the Paris Basin. Radial motorways and TGV (high-speed train) lines meet there, so its hinterland reaches across France.
The first TGV line, Paris to Lyon, opened in 1981. Charles de Gaulle Airport serves the city, and its region, Ile-de-France, has about 12 million people.

London is the capital of the United Kingdom and a global financial centre, through the City of London. Greater London has about 9 million people (Census 2021), and its commuter belt covers much of south-east England.
Brussels is the capital of Belgium and seat of the European Commission and the Council of the EU, so its influence extends across the EU. NATO headquarters is also there.
The European Parliament meets both in Brussels and in Strasbourg, its official seat, so not all EU institutions are in Brussels.
Rotterdam is Europe's largest port, at the mouth of the Rhine (Europoort). Its hinterland is the whole Rhine basin, linked by river barges, rail and pipelines, so it crosses national borders.
Milan is the main city of Lombardy, the core of northern Italy, and Italy's financial centre, home to the Borsa Italiana stock exchange (where company shares are traded).
Other urban regions named in exam matching include Munich (capital of Bavaria), Berlin (capital of Germany) and Rome (capital of Italy).
notes.tip: Say that the European Parliament sits in both Brussels and Strasbourg; do not say all EU institutions are in Brussels. For Rotterdam, use it as the example of a port hinterland crossing national borders. In matching, each named city is the urban region, not an administrative or core region.

notes.h: The Randstad: a polycentric city region
notes.b: Most city regions have one dominant centre, but the Netherlands has a region built around several cities of similar importance.
points: The Randstad in the Netherlands is a ring of cities (Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht) forming one large urban region around a rural area called the Green Heart (Groene Hart).
It is polycentric, meaning it has many centres, in contrast to the single-centre city regions of Paris and Dublin.

keyTerms.definition: A central point where transport routes meet, usually a town or city.
A city and the surrounding area linked to it by flows of people, goods, services and information.
The area around a town or city that it serves and depends on for jobs, shopping, services and markets.
The part of a city's hinterland from which people travel daily to work in the city.
The continuously built-up part of a city.
The largest city in a country, far larger than any other, usually the capital.
A city region with several centres of similar size rather than one dominant city.

questions.prompt: Examine the relationship between an urban area and its hinterland, with reference to an Irish or European city you have studied.
questions.model: Dublin is a nodal region: a primate city linked by flows to the surrounding area. Its urban area is the built-up city, while its hinterland extends far beyond it. Its node status comes from radial national routes meeting at the M50 ring road, the main rail lines, Dublin Port and Dublin Airport. The commuter belt extends into Meath, Kildare, Wicklow and Louth, with commuter towns such as Navan, Naas, Newbridge, Bray and Drogheda. Flows run both ways: commuters travel in to jobs, while the hinterland supplies food, water, raw materials and labour, and the city supplies manufactured goods and services. The city provides shops, hospitals, third-level colleges, entertainment and offices that smaller places cannot support. For government, national media, specialist hospitals and the main airport, the hinterland is the whole country. The hinterland is measured by commuting census data, the catchment areas of hospitals and colleges, the circulation area of local newspapers, bus and rail routes, business delivery areas and the home addresses of shoppers. Its edge is not sharp, because neighbouring hinterlands overlap. It changes over time: motorways, car ownership, faster rail and remote working extend commuter belts. The relationship also brings problems, including urban sprawl, long commutes and congestion, and high house prices.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a nodal region and describe one way the extent of a city's hinterland can be measured.
questions.model: A nodal region is a city together with the surrounding area linked to it by flows of people, goods, services and information, so it is defined by connections rather than by uniform features. One way to measure the hinterland is by the catchment area of a hospital, college or secondary school, which shows the area from which its users come. Other methods include commuting data from the census and the circulation area of a local newspaper.

questions.prompt: True or false: (a) A city's hinterland can be mapped using the circulation area of its local newspaper. (b) A nodal region is defined by features that are the same throughout it.
questions.model: (a) True: the circulation area of a local newspaper shows the area the city's media serves. (b) False: a nodal region is defined by links to a central node, not by features that are the same throughout it.
